title: Oblique Triangles Practice
description: Practice distinguishing right and oblique triangles and identifying given cases.

questions.question: Which statement best describes an oblique triangle?
options: A triangle with three equal sides
A triangle with one angle greater than 180°
questions.explanation: An oblique triangle is any triangle that does not have a right angle.

questions.question: A triangle has angles 42°, 71°, and 67°. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: None of the angles is 90°, so the triangle is oblique. All three angles are less than 90°, so it is acute.

questions.question: A triangle has angles 28°, 62°, and 90°. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: A triangle with one 90° angle is a right triangle, not an oblique triangle.

questions.question: Two angles of a triangle are 38° and 57°. What is the third angle?
A triangle has angles 115°, 30°, and 35°. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: There is no 90° angle, so it is oblique. Since 115° is greater than 90°, it is obtuse.

questions.question: You know all three side lengths of a triangle. Which given case is this?
questions.explanation: Three known side lengths form the SSS case.

questions.question: You know two sides and the angle between them. Which given case is this?
questions.explanation: Two sides with their included angle form the SAS case.

questions.question: You know two angles and the side between those angles. Which given case is this?
questions.explanation: Two angles with the included side form the ASA case.

questions.question: Every obtuse triangle is an oblique triangle.
questions.explanation: An obtuse triangle has one angle greater than 90°, so it cannot have a 90° angle. Therefore it is oblique.

questions.question: For an oblique triangle with SSS information, which strategy is usually useful later?
options: No triangle strategy can be used
questions.explanation: SSS information in an oblique triangle usually points toward the Law of Cosines when solving for an angle.
